He was clearly of opinion that the air corms. at high altitudes were propelled at rates of velocity mot, moody greater than that of any of the swiftest and most terrible tornadoes rec,ded, and that the direction, were fluenced by totally different laws than air currents. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 1(I, MO.

Another chapter in the history of the interminable Eastern Question has been almoat completed. The Sublime Porte, clever or it iv in diplomatic intrigue, bee been over-reached in its attempt to play a deep end desperate game with the six Great Power. of Europe; and despite the bold front it put on only a few days ego, it has done that which we atated in the Bromine, last week it would do, namely, eat the proverbial leek. The Porte believed it could nomad, by its vacillation and its conditional refusal to fulfil the pledgee it made to the Berlin Congress, in sowing disunion and jealouay among the Powers acting in concert; but by forwarding the impudent note it did to the Great Powers it unwittingly strengthened the bonds of union between the nations which had determined that the Sick Man of the Porte, the common disturber of European peas*, should no longer belie his promises made at the Betlin Congress The "tail end" of the Conservative party in England have played as sorry a figure in this last chapter of the Eastern Question as the Sublime Porto itself. Little more than two yours have elapsed sines Jingoism wee in full swing in England, and the spirited foreign policy exemplified by the Beaconsfield Government was proclaimed from the house tope is the one to settle the Eastern grievance for ever. The Berlin Congrem woe one of the fruits of that Govern- ment's filibustering policy, and when that Congress ' had impoeed upon Turkey certain obligationa affecting the partitioning of its European Kingdom, and Turkey herself had given a solemn promise to the Congress to comply with thaw obligations, England's repreeen- Wives at the Congress returned home with a nourish of trumpets, and avowed that they had feastred peace with honour. So long, however, or dog

Ommervative Government remained in power no attempt whatever w made either on the part of Turkey to carry cow her pledgee, or on the part of any of the Great Powen, to compel her to fulfil the terms of their deciaion. The spirited foreign policy hod no for supplied a certain amount of glitter to the chief wire pullers of the Conservative party, and it had served to laminate excitable Jingoes, pleased with a bauble for an hour. There was, however, no real practical busineee associated with the declaration of peace with honour, and it remained for Mr. Glad- stone, when be came into power, to see to it that the expense the couutry had incurred in defraying the poet of the grand proceesional tour of the English plenipotentiarim to Berlin, and that the solemn deliberations of the statesmen of the different European nationalities, did not end in a fares. Whm he set to work with a view to finishing the labours hie prede- oemons bad begun, and to induce Turkey to abandon her offs-government and net her boom in order, the active spirits of the Conservative party were strong in their oondemnation of Mr. Gladstone aspiring to put • firdahing touch to the work they had inaugurated but practically left a dead letter. Though, in the interesta of Enema and of all Europe, Mr. Gladstone eucceeded in convincing the statesmen of the chief nationalities that Turkey must be compelled to fulfil her obligation, if the Governmmta of Europe were to be eared from being placed in a ridiculous position, and if the Eastern Question had to be kept from perpetuating rivalries and jealousies among diplomatists, the course pursued unhappily by a auction of the Conservative party has too clearly mani• faded that they would have been ready to [hail inn jubilant epirit even the humiliation of their own wintry if they cotild only have had their wither gratified that Mr. Gladstone should meet at the hands of the Powers acting in concert with contempt and ridicule. We do not profess that there can have been any connection between those Conservatives actuated by this spirit and the advisers of the Sultan, but it Is somewhat eingular that whilst the Sultan should have believed that by putting on a bold front andi defying the Powers acting in coneert he would be ambled to row dissension among these Powers, the Conservatives here should have been praying for the realisation of such an event. The latter, however, have been disappointed, and the Turks hare dis- covered that their days of trickery in Enropean polities are drawing to an end. Once convinced of the earnestness of the European concert, and that the Englieh Government was sonimated by a different epirit to that which moved the Beacons- field Cabinet, the Sublime Porte suddenly die. revered that discretion was the better part of colour; and, rather than eubmit to have Smyrna and Salonica or Beyrout occupied by the allied fleets, and the port revenues fieqemetrated, she quickly signified her intention to hand over to the /I ootenegrine the fort of Dulcigno in peace. 'netted of putting forward conditions in a bumptious and arro- gant note affecting the transfer of Thessaly and Zpirtm to Greece, and the execution of reforms in • Armenia, Turkey, in a humble spirit, naked the allied Powers not to peen for the present the settlement of thaw pending queetione. Mr. Martin Taylor, the Prime Minister, read the Queen's speech, which wars as fellows : Gentlemen,—lt givee me great pleasure and satisfaction to have thie opportunity of meeting you after the recent general electron, and the arrangements required upon a change of adminietratien. My relations with foreign Powers are friendly, and I trust, in concert with the other Powers parties to (hr Berlin Treaty, to bring shout an early and complete fulBlment of that treaty, both as regards the necee- eery re-arrangement of frontiers, as well as effectual reforms and equal law. in Turkey, so that the countries which hare been in a state of oppression and disorder may have the bletrings of peace encored to them. Towards the accain• pliehment of these matters, I have sent an Envoy Extra- ordinary to Constantinople, and, by agreement with the great Powers have directed some of my ships to the waters of Dolcigno. lam pleased no be able to announce a com- plete settlement of the Zulu difficulty ; and I have hopes that the difficulties in Basutoland will be speedily settled with due regard to the rights and liberties of all the peoples intereeted. I congratulate you on the pacific direction in which events in Afghanistan ion tending, and whilst re- grating the waste of life and treasure that has taken place in that country, I hope to establish friendly relations with all the tribes. The condition of the finances In India will be laid before you, and measures for goal propoeed, which I hope will place that part of my dominions in • more pros prams and contented condition. I notice with andantino that the trade of the country and the revenue are inn fair way towards permanent recovery. The estimates will be trained with due regard to economy, and will be laid before you as soon as possible. Measurer; will be provided for the improvement of the condition of Ireland, end I hope that the unhappy otate of that country will give place to one of contentment and prosperty. Are bmosserno Cone TO WIIINIL9 Here.—At Bt. Helens County Court, on Wednesday last, John Power, a fumaceman, of Widnea, Cued Messrs. Eccles Bros., chemical manufacturers, Widnes, for £2 Is. &I. for wages stopped by way of fine, and for a week's wages in lieu of notice —Mr. Husband appeared for the plaiotiff, and Mr. Swift for the defendanta.—lt appeared that, on Sunday night, the sth September, plaintiff went to his work at five o'clock. He complained to the foreman that his furnace was choked. The foreman told him to get it heated, and be would be allowed two lionss. Plaintiff only got two bane out by Mx o'clock on Monday morning, wben he left the works. When he returned to work the same evening, he found a man in his place, and he was taken to Mr. Walker, the manager who gave him Se., pert of wages due, and retained 10s. ed. as a Rae for alleged neglect for not getting more balls, and dismirsed him. Power sued for this 10s. dd. and £1 Ifs. for • week's wages for wrongful dismissal.—The defendants, by a eel-off, claimed SA be. damages for wrongfully and in. properly neglecting his work, and causing saute, loan, and damage to his employers, and called Mr. Martin (the fore- man) and • mixer to prove that the plaintiff was lying down asleep during the night shift, and Mr. Walker to prove the damage.—His Honour, Mr. Thompson, gave plaintiff a vet- diet for the 10s. &I. stopped, and 14a. M. for days lost up to the time when plaintiff obtained other employment at the " Desoto" works, and dismissed the defendant's counter.

COLONEL IRRI.AND Bxrclizossa, M.P., ON nce &nom BOARD Srsram.—Colonel Ireland Blackburn°, M.P. for Booth-Weat Lancashire, on Wednesday opened a bazaar in the Cambridge Hall, Southport, in aid of the North Meals Parish Church Schools. In the course of his remarks he observed that, warmly attached as he was to the voluntary principles of education, he attended there with the greateat possible pleasure. Although he was free to confess that there were Immo towns in which School Board, were neces- sary and desirable, dill he held against the doctrine a establishing such Boards all over the country. It would encourage and engender all aorta of ill-feeling with regard to differeat schools, and he thought the managers of thoee schools were better able to succeed than if they had then School Boards in the country. (Hear, hear.) He considered that education without religion was more than useless—in fact, that it was positively wrong; and he remarked that those who worked for the children should see that religioas education was inculcated in their minds.

PERFORMANCE OF " THE FLOWER QUEEN," AT RUNCORN. Some time ego the friends connected with the Beam& Congregadonal church, Runcorn, which under the pastorate of the Rev. J. D. Thomas appears to be very flourishing, determined to commence • movement for the purpose of supplementing the minister's fend, and ultimately raising a suficient snm to pay the rent of the mienter's reeidence. This proposal wan favourably received, and considerable dis- cussion took place as to the Plan to be adopted for the pur- pose of raising the money. Mr. Tunolh, who is an ardent admirer of Mr. Cerwen'e system of musical notation, said he should he glad it they could me their way to icing out a musical composition entitled "The Flower Queen, or the Coronation of the Rose," by Mr. Ii F. Root, of Chicago, the libretto being by Min Frances J.Crosby, the blind deleriol poetess. Me. Tonnah, is mentioning the matter, remarked that some yore ago he lived in Stothport, and be 'minced e Mr. Bradbury to join him in giving the piece in connection with the Toiric Sol-fa Anocistion. He afterwards removed to %cup, and eocceeded in getting the Congregational church at that place to give the performance, which Proved sotsucceeeful that it was repestedeeveral times. The proposal wm adopted by the church at Bethesda, and the friende threw themselves into the carrying of the rbeme with much energy. About three months were devoted to the training of thom who had tonke pert in it but the success with which the production wse received at the Public Hall on Wednesday evening, must hare proved ample rewardlo thoee who had /Mown to mod, patience in the work. Before proceeding any further, it may be of interest to give a sketch of " The Flower Queen," forth, proper carry- ing out of which a platform profusely decoratet with planta andflower, to give it the appearance of a dell in the formt, Is needed, the fair singers being suitably attired wering the particular flower each represents. A brilliant overture rommencm the Cantata, and when the curtain rises, the whole of the flowers are discovered assembled 10 the dell to chose their Queen, this. is followed by a full chorus, descriptive of the flowers near the clom of the chorus, a distant footetep is heard and they leave in haste. A person discontented with the world now entre the dell, and being charmed with in beauty, ropretere his dmire to remain there, In the words, " There would I rest," he. He is invited by thismund of distant voices to remain and take up hie abode. He expresses his wonder and astonishment in song, whence the munch proceed, when .o , of the flowers appear, and intimate in a charming duet that I it is the mmic of the flowers. The flowers then re-aseemble 1 in the dell to choose their Queen. In a number ot beautiful ergs each avpirant puts forth her claim to the crown. Many 00th, eongs have a well-arroniged choral smornpani- mot, prominent amongst them being the " Sunflower," 1 which is exceedingly effective and racy. But before the choice in concluded eight come, on, and a troop of "Pimple." enter and lull them to sleep with the subtle narcotic. A hymn dedicated to'Night, by the flowers, ac-; companied in song by the Recluse, appropriately brings the first day to • dose. At the break of day they again assemble, and 10 (011 chorus wish each other `qr.! morn- ing." Several other flowers then prefer their claim, after hearing which, they appeal to the Recluse to decide for them. Los suitable song he canteens the difficulty of choosing, "where uature's hand alike her gifts bestow," bet in conclusion snorers the "Rose " their Queen, to which ' they unanimously give their anent. Having sang the i chorus "Prepare we for the testi, scene" they return to make preparation for the coronation. A bevy of little girls then enter repreeenting the " limtber bells" and greet the dowers in • lively chortle. All the flowers then appear and : sing • grand coronation march, after which four 01 the I flowers advance to the loot of the throne, and palm the coronet on the brow of the Queen elect, when the ascends , her throne, the flowen tmtifying their joy in Me beautiful I chorus, "Long lin oar beauteous Queen." The Rector having expressed hie intention of returning too life sf use- fulness and couteetment, the last grand chorus, "Light of eternal love" brings the Cantata to a clom.

The annual meeting of the Runcorn auxiliary of the British and Foreign Bible Society was held on Tuesday ! evening, in the ante-room of the Public Hall, that town. ! The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were also pre- ' mat .—The Revs J. Nowell, W. Preston, MA. Evan Williams, T. The sudden death of 31r. J. Page, who I wee so well known as the society's secretary, wee referred to In teeing terms. Looking at the operations of the branch in Runcorn, • change for the better had been made. During the last twelve months they had had no colporteur at mock; but he hoped that before the end of the preeent year they would have one canvassing in the town. He was glad to report that the system of separate auxiliary branchee attached to each church and chasml in the district, in the plam of mveml independent collectors deputed to collect where and how they best could, (introduced by the We Mr. Page) con- tinued no work efficiently and effectively. He did not per- ceive any falling off in the contribution.. If any enciety claimed their sympathy, demanded their support, and re- gaited their aid, it was the British and Foreign Bible Society, for without it they would be moding their brave mis- sionaries to fight either with tied hande or without needful wexpo!,!e. . .

Onoe the Bible was entirely in the hands of the priesthood, and copies of it could only be found in the libraries of cathe- drals or convents. (Applause.) The advocates of elninentary eduntion in our day had far fewer didiculties to contend with than the Avocates of elementary education had to coutend with some years ago. There were very few people now to deny the advantage of education. but be remembered the time, even in his comparatively !Mort life, when educa- tion was considered by no means an unmixed good, if not • rml evil. It was thought if working people were educated they would be less docite, not so easily managed, more akillid to do evil and perhope hue willing to do well. And it was thought in those days that whatever might be the Coon in reference to other classes of society, It was very doubtful whether the working dames were better for educa- tion. He had • friend of bibs minister, who did not hesi- tate to ear to him on one occasion that he thought that ignorant people were much mom easily taught, were much [lmre teachable than if they knew more, and his friend rather deprecated the education of the labouring clamee on that account. I Hear, hear.) Those ideas as to the evils of education had, however, been long exploded, bathe thought it posaible,and indeed perhaps probable, that the future historian of our time. would think It remarkable that in this country no national system of eduration worthy of the name existed until the year 1870. Itt addition to that there was on improymneut in the quality, the education was much better than I.e remembered it to have been when he was young. The great drawhlck en far.,, be knew with regard to the education of the young—he was Speaking more par- ticularly of the elementary education of the young—was that what they learned in the school was not followed up after they left school. (Hear, hear.) Ile believed in his village and mill the young people knew mom at 13 years of age than they did at 20. NEWTON AND FARLESTOWN. NRIVTOII-LB-WILLOWS CHORAL Somerv.—This society has entered upon its winter session with • mecobership largely increased over that of last year. Thanks ts the zee of the conductor, Mr. P. Fairclough, and the efficiency of the members, the inhabitaots of Newton enjoyed a very pleasant concert at the close of the last musical session, and if the reciely could see Haney to repeat that successful ex- periment two or three times during the approaching dull season • great benefit would be conferred upon the com- munity. The membem meet for practice every Monday night in the school rooms, Mercer-street. WESLEYAN Tonto Men's Mr-reALlovlTMeder B.mm—the winter semen of this flourishing society •ill be formally opened this (Saturday) evening, at a soiree to be held in the schoolroom under the old chapel. After entertaining their friends and Chewer'ss to tea, • concert interopented with recitations will be given by the members, who will have the valuable assistance of Miss Swan, Mr. Swan, junr., ant Mr. Thomas Stanfield, the latter being a very efficient though modest player of the violin. A capital aeries of papem is arranged teethe coming session. The secretary is Mr. Peter Parr, who will be happy to receive the names of intending members. EAELBS,WIE AND DISTRICT !ANIMAL CLEW—Though the club premises were thrown open to members without cere- mony a fortnight ago, the committee proposes to formally inaugnrate the club at • meeting to he held either at the end of the month or early in November. The exact date is not yet determined, bat the 30th October is spoken of ae the most likely day. A eubstantial tea is to be provided at the nominal cOst of a ehilling a head, and the committee hope that as many of the members as can will make a point of attending. George McCorquodale, Esq., will preside, end eeveral of the leading liberals of Liverpool end the district are expected to be present amongst other., Mn. Herbert Gladstone, eon of the Premier, has been writttn to. The success of the club has so far excesled all expectation.. more than two hundred membere having joined and the greater part of the shares being already taken op. '[he political secretary of the Club claims a gam of fifty for the Liberals at the recent division of voters for the Newton totem I chip. ---AC;Ccouc ARCHBISHOP'S ADVICE vo rite Intart Paola. —Dr. SlTabe, the Catholic Archbishop of Dublin, hm in- n-ood en important pastoral to the clergy on the 'deo of Ire. land. He says perialic famine. wills which the people are continually threatened, the inaccurity of their and ',rime, which paralyses the most industrious hands, and the wretchol condition of thousands of tamale., whose domestic arrangements might test the temper of a slave-coast African, all proclaim that the land laws require a prompt and thorough revision. The management of public affairs, be continues, is now placed in the hands of men who seem to have the most abundant goodwill to redress the wrongs of the country, as far as a Government can accomplish nth a work. Guarantees for the sincerity of their good wishes are furnished by their antecedents. Their determination to carry on the affairs of Ireland by laws in harmony with con. Mitutiunal liberty has been made manifest. They have also repudiated the idea of coercion. But how, lie asks, has this generous and unusual moderation been men? Men who claimed the high honour of being leaders of the people were not ashamed to proclaim that they wonld render the country unfit for constitutional liberty by making it reverts. able by constitutional inems Is this the policy by which the people ue to he led to freedom and prosperity ? They have heard propounded by these Same men, no doubt in ail , sincerity, schema of amelioration of such an order that no Government laying claim to RlAlE9lllAnship could for a moment entertain them. The unhappy country has within the last few months drunk deoply of the blood of their own children. Let the wine nod moderate men of the country I arrange a plan of action which God can bless, awl then it , will not be many years before justice shall spring up and peace and plenty take their lasting abode amongst them. SUMAC/in On 'rue Caine—At a meeting of the Birmingham Reform League on Thursday night, a letter wan read from Mr. A. M. Sullivan, M.P, in which the honourable member declared that the mote of affairs in Ire- land was very aerione, and not an ordinary political move- ment. It was the great, wild, passionate uprising of a peo- ple filled with the desperate purpose of tearing down and destroying the feudal eystem which had no long oppressed them. He had never before known the Irish people no roused. Things were said and done which every man of calm mind most deplore, but when a whole people were in such a mood, it were folly and sheer childislaneas to marvel at incidents of pamion and violence. div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

A epecial Meeting of this Board was held on Thursday afternerm. Mr. R. Bradshaw presided, and there were also preheat Meagre. Robert Shaw, W. Hartland, U. Taylor, It. Itemiser, T. S. 'Jimmie, H. W. Deacon, Dr. O'Keeffe, and G. H. Denby (clerk). The meeting was called for the purpose of passing the statement of receipts and expenditure for the year endiog the 29th ult. Mr. Slum, chairman of the Finance Committee, pre- sented the atatement of accounts, and mid it bad net usual to offer any rernarks unless they contained somethieg of an exceptio.l character. 'llse only thing he need refer , to wee the fact that there were the salaries of thirteen montha. in the statement, so that in comparing it with that of last year they would have to deduct £259. Tins would make the expenditure similar to thst of the previous year. He might say th.ct the amount required for rating purposes had been tonne amide, and they had about £1,150 to receive on, the precept. lie thought it was wise for the Board when hewing the precept to ask force amount which they thought they wotild require, inatead of issuing two or three Precept. during the veer. div.head: STRANGE DROWNING CASE AT
div.p: STRANGE DROWNING CASE AT
DUTTON.
On Thursday, ningrTasi ;rl;a-held at the Talbot Arms, Dutton, by Mr. T. J. Ridgway, coroner, touching the death of Ann Colclough, whooo body woc found in the ea.l at lltaton.

Thomas Coiclough said: I live in Aston, near Dutton, and am the tunnel keeper on the canal. The body the jury have seen is that of my wife, Ann Colelough. She was 57 years of age. I last now her alive about eight o'clock on the evening of the 4th instant. I went out of the house, leaving my wife on the mole. She appeared to be asleep. I went out to attend to my werk. I went back to the house soon afterwards, but found the door locked, and I then thought my wife wart out. One of my lodgers told me he thought my wife had gone to Sandbach. She had a sister at Sand. barb, and has been in the habit of going there. I then broke the door open, but my wife was not in the house. On the return of the boat from Sandbach in which I thought my wife had gone, I was told she had not gone. I had also written to Sandbach and got a similar reply. I began dragging the meal, and on Sunday lart I found her lamp. I confine.] dragging, and on the 12th October I found the body of my wife in the canal (the Brent and Mersey canal), about 50 yards from my door near tunnel top. The deceased had been poorly fer the last em x month., and has been under Dr. Latham, a Sandbach. She suffered front bile on the liver, and at times complained of great pain, and teas de- pressed. She had complained of being very poorly on the 4th October. The body seas properly dresied when I found it. The hourt key was in bee pocket. John Harrison stoical: I live at Ettley Heath, near Sand- bar!), and am a Lebow*r. On the 4th instant I was lodging , at the boom of Thome. Colclough, at tunnel top. I was in the house a little after eight o'clock on the evening of °actor 4th. Mrs. Colclough wasl lying on the sofa. I went to bed about ten minutes poet eight. I mid "Good night" to deceased, and she mid "moral night, John." There was no one el. in I boom. I then went up to bed, and I got into bed in a few minutes. Before I went to [deep I thought I heard the de- ceased talking, hot whether she was talking to herself or someone else Ido not know. I have beard her talk to her- self. I did not hear anyone come into the house or go out of it. I went to eleep in about three-quarters of an hour. I did not know the deceased had gone out until ibbween Band 10 o'clock the same evening, when my bedfellow, Jobe. Tur- ner, came to bed and told me. Deceased had complained of being poorly. I had seen deceased tipsy a time or two, but am not able to say whether ahe was tipsy or not on the evening of the 4th October. Herbert Potm, the younger, check clerk for the North Stafford Railway Company, said he eaw the bodv pulled out of the renal and assisted to remove it. The deceased was not a very steady woman. Mary Ann Botts, wife of Herbert Potts, sen., agent for the North stafford Canal, said Ole laid out the body. There were no marke of violence on the body, excepting a not on the outside of the left leg, just above the knee, which in her opinion was caused after death. The jury returned a verdict of *Booed drowned." WARRINGTOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

In attendance at the Workhouse school there were 106 boys and 78 girls, At whom 40 boys and 48 girls were receiving industrial training.

At a meeting of the above committee, held on the 12tli October, Mr. filackhurst in the chair, the Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board requesting to be in. formed of the result at which the Guardians might arrive on the exception taken by Mr. Motley, school inspector, to the exceuive amount of making and mending articles of clothing at present executed in the girls' school. Mrs. Mackey explained that she could net supply further help from the W.C.liouse. There being now ILI children at the Schools, the committee agreed that the amount of sewing work was great, and that assistance was required. With a view to obtaining the proportion of salary an industrial trainer Appointed with the approval of the Local Govern- ment Board receives from Parliamentary grants, it was agreed to recommend the appointment of aa indukrial trainer, whose duty it should be to nuke clothes as well as to repair them, the following resolution was Nosed: —.That with a view to meet the irregularities and defects to which Mr. Moxley, echool inspector, has taken exception and to eupply the wanted aulstance in the making and mend- nag of articles of clothing, at preeent executed in the girls' ached, the Local Government Board be requested to approve the appointment of an additional female industrial trainer. whose duties shall be to take charge of the sewing. mending of children's clothes, and other situilar work, and to instruct the girls in duties of that kind." The committee proceoded to sonsidet tlie appointment of a superintendent. at lequired ' by the new regulation, Mr. Mines (schoolmaster) ...I called before the committee, Ind he replied that he eras, Ware what the duties were, and if the Guardians appointed him he would toihl the duties to the best of his ability. It was resolved that he he appointed superintendent of the schools, and that a salary of £lO a year be paid to him for his services. Mine Walton was called into the room, and eaid she would have pleasure to fulfil the duties of matron, if no required by the Guardians. It seas resolved—. That Mien Walton be Ap;minted matron of the schools." Miss Jones was also called before the committee, and informed of the proposed alterations in the management of the schools. As the above minutes involved the tranctioniog of expen- diture, the Cr. arta said notice would have to he given to each Guardian, and until that was done the nainutee could not be diacusecd. this was all the bueinese.

Hough said that on the night in question he went let° Mr. Bailey's house, the Aston Arms, when one of the prisoners said," Have you come here ss a spy ?" and be said." He ultimately managed to fight his way Oat, and ran towards home. However, before he eould get into the house he was again knocked down and kicked, on which he screamed "Mender." P.C. The officer'e head was bleeding, and, in consequence of what he (Speed) said, hr sent him on to Runcorn, and went near to the Weaver with the other officer who was with him, and hid. He they heard some men walk- ing along the road as if they were coming from Frodsham Bridge. The other three prisoners immediately came up, and they took them into cuatody. A fight then took place, and Hough was knocked down.—The Chairman .aid they had no doubt about the assault having been committed, and it was a most outrageous one. GETTTOODY.--On Thurs- dav, the Rev. J. Guttridge preached a sermon in the above chapel. and in the evening delivered his popular lecture in the Town Hall, Frodshatn, entitled, .1 he necessity of elevernew—the greater neceasity of goodness" when Mr. A. White, of llelsby, presided, and the proceeds were in aid of the funds of the Frudsharn Primitive Methodist Chapel. The rev. lecturer stated that a great man is greater than • great city. Homer and Virgil,lHerodolus and Cicero, Plato and Socrates, were gr.ter than either Nephir or Theb., Carthage or Idabylon, Athens or Rome. Mind fadial not sway with the receding ages. Matter, though upon it mind may tare left its artistic traces, went down to decay. •, Stately temples, shrine* of gold, Psi-4111dr a‘y!oyy LBW,

The gift, raid ftc l'e-cf";;;;,. 1,;-ille.;,:o-r1,1:1'• great man can ! never be over rated. Its price I. above rubies. Such • man stands before the intellect and heart of the many around ! him, his mission being to educate both, lie suffers not by , contrast. The thinkers of the ages have been the bene- factors of the ages. The few think, the many are thought- , less. The lower rulea over the higher self ; the animal dominates over the angel; passion is eovereign ; he is, ! therefore, the true and strong man who, having with , humanity sympathy, seeks to adjust it. Bacon's aphorism ! wears well, its accuracy remains, '• Knowledge is power." , An ignorant man is easentially a weak man. Ignorance too it proverbislly hampering. it is exceedingly inconvenient ; not to know. To be opulent in ideas is better , than to be opulent in gold. The brain bank . is better than Rothschilds. There is less risk and more certain return.. The mental millionaire is immesaureably superior to the monetary one. He who is ; only worth money is almost worthless. Wealthy men differ , very widely, hence there are refined rich men who are . mainly known for their ample resources and elegant habits. j Many uf these have heads as soft as their hands and there , are ill-informed men, rude rich men, who would confound , .• Magna Charts" with the a Bill of Rights" and would , not know distinctly hoer wide was the moral chasm between , Henry VIII. and Albert the Good. The term clever is rather , elastic. it is sometimes used to indicate a little evanescent , sprightliness associated with very high and reprehensible , airs; hence we say of a fumy but really illiterate man "tie is too clever by half." At other times it is employed to dicate substantial work, intellectual /debility, and trust- worthiness. In such cases we qualify the word and say of . sack a nian that he is really clever, supposing by that way of putting it that there is around as a great deal of empty , in lieu of solid work. But the men who are really clever are not all equally so. Sometimes., meet with one who I stands out most distinctly, who separates himself 8010 the j many around him by his not moderate but immense capacity. He it not low anywhere; he is or in everything, clever all round. Some are clever as speakers, but they are . poor as thinkers. They are disinclined to study the abtose ; . they have no taste at all for the intellectually hard and un- , yielling. They sae they cannot study well, and of them- ! /wives they report accurately. Others are clever as thinkers, • but poor as apeakers. Some have a highly educated . and logical consciousness, but they seem void . of sensation. They are hard as rocks, cold , as winter, and unmovable as marble. Som, , know a little and that little well. Others seem se, if they knew everything. You cannot put them in an awkward position or moot a subject upon which their thoughts have not been expended. No one ever saw them when they looked silly, indeed ae a rule they looked more sagacione than I "any man" ever really was. They have no unguarded .1 moments, no Mimi side, they are not caught napping. They are wide awaks they do not give you life in the leaflet, in , the lovely page, or isolated essay. They are encyclopawlias I This was said, if I mistake not, of Lord Thurlow. of this ,I class the ages are very sparing. They come at long intervals. , They are stars of the first magnitude, Oat shine in com- paratively lonely splendour; and when we have them we can scarcely be too grateful for them. It is not in the power of either low ribaldry er cultured acorn, of cool ignorement or bitter malignity to either interest, curb, or cruah their ! influence. Lift them to the sommit of the official mountain ; or leave them at its base; put them in office or keep them cot. Still there is no real dethronement by others, nor effective atslication by themselves. They retain the purple they reign on. They may even die, but death is not equal Ito their dismissal from office, or the curtailment of their power. Age after age fails either to Impair their high authority or hush their arrestive eloquence. Being dead, they ',peak. They seethe princes of our kind ; the monarchs of our arrive; King of God's own anointing, net Apart that they might on all grave questions minister to the dignity aed well being of myrails. Of our poor humanity, they are the nobleet type. The vase seems to have no flow; , the pet of precioue ointment no fly the monument no duet; and the sun no spots. ! They xern robe without rents nips or vacancies, amply Plied up, fully developed, extraordinary men. Now the man who answers to this deacription as much if not more then any other in either England, Europe, or the world, is ; our esteemed William Ewart Gladstone. (Applauae.) From this attitude we must, however, descend, atel seek to clasaife a few who are clever not in everything but in what is usually termed their own department. The lecturer then proceeded to speak of the poetically clew, the critically clever, the satirically clever, the quoMtively clever, the biratically clever, thew clever at repartee and instanter replies, the proverbially clever, ho.; and stated that from what he had said it was evident that society offend for our inspection. =Orli, and dissection every variety of sapacity. It also offered every variety of character, because there were those who were undoubtedly elever, but that was all they could , say of them. There their eulogy ended, for that was in re- lation to Glen, tie far end. They were great without being I good. The lecturer here enumerated the men who came under this description, and treated this part of the subject in an able, forcible, and exh”stive manner. The usual vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the proceedings to • close.
